claims.text: The proposed model integrates DFT-derived atomic-scale descriptors with descriptors of the HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure.
A machine-learning model can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing.
The model will predict all three mechanical properties with less than 15% error relative to experiments.
The model will be at least 10 times faster than traditional full-scale simulations.
As-cast HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with nanoscale phase separation, such as a ductile matrix containing precipitates.
Tensile and fracture tests will be conducted under quasi-static loading at approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Testing will cover room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures.
The distribution and morphology of nanoscale phases in the hierarchical microstructure influence elastic and plastic responses.
Elastic constants, misfit volumes, phase fractions, and microstructural morphology govern dislocation behavior and fracture mechanisms.
Using these descriptors enables the model to capture the effect of hierarchical heterostructuring on macroscopic mechanical performance.
The model eliminates the need for computationally expensive full-scale simulations.
Conventional full-scale DFT or finite-element simulations are accurate but require considerably more computational time and resources.
Predictive accuracy may deteriorate when the tested microstructure differs substantially from microstructures represented in the training data.
Unexpected phase transformations or defect concentrations may place the material outside the model's reliable domain.
The approach may fail if DFT-derived parameters do not capture non-equilibrium effects during testing.
Predicted values have an inherent uncertainty of approximately 10–15% because of experimental variability and incomplete representation of complex microstructural effects.
The validation experiment will use more than 10 HfNbTiVAl10 samples and measure Young's modulus, yield strength, fracture toughness, and computational time.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if any predicted property differs from experiment by more than 15% or if the speedup is less than 10-fold.

contradictions.description: The performance claim requires error strictly below 15%, but the falsification rule triggers only when error exceeds 15%. An error of exactly 15% would violate the stated hypothesis without satisfying the declared falsification rule.
